newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England sees big benefits from EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England sees big benefits from EMU.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George believes European monetary union offers huge opportunities for London as a financial centre, whether or not Britain signs up, according to an interview published on Monday.
But he told the Financial Times newspaper that disagreements over some important banking issues between Germany and France, the stalwarts of monetary union, and Britain could be damaging.

Two opinion polls, also released on Monday, showed a majority of British business leaders oppose a single currency, believing it would damage the British economy, while most ordinary people say the country should keep its options open.
George said European economic and monetary union (EMU) could be "an absolutely huge opportunity" for the City of London, Europe's biggest financial centre.
"I think the potential pluses are very considerable in relation to the potential minuses."

But this was based on the assumption that the technical preparations for monetary union would be in place and that current negotiations on the details proceeded in a "constructive, mutual-interest kind of way."

George said some French and German banks wanted to see countries which remain outside EMU excluded from equal access to a new inter-bank payments system known as Target in order to give themselves a competitive advantage.
"For the first time something has been introduced into the EMU discussion which is discriminatory for a non-monetary reason," he said.

"This could change the nature of the debate. It would move from a constructive environment where people were all working together to one where people were in a different game of protecting national interests."

The central bank chief said he would very much regret any change to the constructive environment in which the EMU process has been conducted until now, but Britain was "not in the business of compromise over Target."
The Maastricht Treaty on European union gives Britain the right to "opt out" of a single currency.
Government policy is to take part fully in preparations for EMU, which is due to start in 1999, while reserving any decision on participation until the project starts up.
The right wing of the ruling Conservative party bitterly opposes the single currency as an unacceptable erosion of British sovereignty.
The Financial Times interpreted the tone of George's remarks as suggesting he expected Britain to be among the "outs" -- the countries which do not participate.
An opinion poll of 392 directors of companies listed on the London Stock Exchange showed 58.4 percent opposed monetary union on the grounds that it would be bad for the British economy.

"Even among the 37.2 percent who support the idea, there are plenty who think Britain should exercise its opt-out clause and postpone adoption of the euro beyond 1999," Hemmington Scott, who conducted the poll for accountants Price Waterhouse, said.

More than 57 percent of those surveyed thought taxes would go up, 42 percent expected government borrowing to soar, 40.8 percent believed prices would rise and 39.5 percent expected interest rates to increase.

A separate poll of British people by the MORI polling organisation for the European Movement showed 60 percent of respondents wanted the government to keep open the option of joining EMU, while only 30 percent favoured ruling it out now, as the Conservative right is urging.
